26. Tablinum (i), N wall, middle area, central aedicule, detail: black predella decorated with grotesques with a satirical protome in the centre, from which symmetrical shoots start. A pardalid hangs from the shoots under the protome. The scrolled shoots ending in ram protomes include a pair of panthers facing a crater chalice; the terminal volutes end up in an elephant protome.
27. Tablinum (i), detail of the predella in the previous figure. Graphic restitution from Mau.

28. Tablinum (i), N wall, middle area, central aedicule, detail: epistyle surmounted by a window on an Ionic colonnade thòlos, with a coffered dome and a leafy central ocular (opaìon). The vertical E-shaped strip of the aedicule is adorned with ellipses with heads alternating with ovals.

29. Tablinum (i), N wall, section E, middle area, detail. The palm trunk that separates the central aedicule from the suspended side carpet is flanked by four pairs of animals in a heraldic position, the highest pair are canids leaning against the back. The vertical strip O of the side panel is adorned (from top to bottom) with an ellipse with a crouching monkey at the back, an amphora, an ellipse with a griffin protome, and a rustic tortoise-shaped lyra with a head on the resonance box.

30. Tablinum (i), N wall, section E, middle area, detail: upper edge of the suspended carpet with peacock feathers surmounted by a box with two tragic masks, supported by the wings of a pair of falcons holding a garland in their beaks. The thyrsis that support the shell are flanked by corymbs.

35-36. Tablinum (i), N wall, section E, middle area, details. The lateral, vegetal edges of the suspended carpet are interrupted, at mid-height, by a branch with a feline climbing it: on the left it seems to be a lion, on the right it is a panther behind it towards the center of the wall or panel.

35-36. Tablinum (i), N wall, section E, middle area, details. The lateral, vegetal edges of the suspended carpet are interrupted, at mid-height, by a branch with a feline climbing it: on the left it seems to be a lion, on the right it is a panther behind it towards the center of the wall or panel.

37. Tablinum (i), wall E, area above the passage to the peristyle: the painting, the only preserved upper section of the tablinum, is no longer in situ. Mau already regrets the loss of the upper area of the N and S walls, where only the preparation layer is preserved. The area above architrave E includes a central white panel with still life in the centre, flanked by garlands and 'ellipses' filled with animals and heads. In the N side panel there are porticoes with two orders of overlapping columns; the columns thicken to the right, to increase the suggestion of depth. The motif 'precedes' the royal portico of the peristyle (1).

38. Tablinum (i), wall E, S-shaped pillar of the passage to the peristyle. The black predella depicts an animal, under the scrolled semicircle. The lotus frame above, and the cylindrical base of the candelabrum adorned with palmettes and meanders of battlements can now be read only in Mau's graphic rendering (see fig. 39). The long, narrow yellow compartment (once cinnabar) is flanked by white strips decorated in an inverted V; the right strip is part of the blue pillar (black monochrome in the Mau plate), which turns the corner and is continuous and does not pretend mirrors. The candelabra compartment is surmounted by a frame of ornate ovals, alternating with lotuses. The picture with ducks in the upper black frieze is flanked by rosettes. The fresco is applied to bricks. The left margin of the-. the plaster was close to the wooden jamb of the door, whose ganghero was fixed in the square recess of the marble threshold.
39. Tablinum (i): wall E, pillar, middle area. Graphic rendering by Mau W.

40 a-b. Tablinum (i), S. The N and S side walls suffered more in the W sections, more exposed to the temperature variations of the sun and the humidity of the rains that fell on that side. The upper edge of the fresco is consolidated with winged nails, according to the nineteenth-century system in use during the excavation period. The rough plaster above belongs to the stucco frame and to the upper area of the fresco, which has not survived.
41. Tablinum (i), S face, E and central section. The graphic rendering from Mau W, tav. XIII coincides with the best preserved part today.  from Mau W, tav. XIII

42. Tablinum (i), S wall, extreme E section, middle area, detail. On the left is the blue pillar that turns the corner (see fig. 38). From the vertical, vegetal edge of the suspended carpet (but one would say a rod) corymbs and ivy leaves sprout on the black background of the side band, which has been pressed before the miniaturist motifs were executed: so the black color has been better preserved than in the rest of the bottom of the band. In tav. XIII of Mau the corymbs also appear on the cinnabar of the carpet: if the restitution is correct, they have disappeared on both walls together with the cinnabar, leaving no traces. The rod is topped by a swan, which holds the carpet rope suspended in its beak. The peacock feathers of the edge of the carpet are joined by inverted arches with a purple background, on which a yellow ivy leaf appears at each feather. The falcons above the shell hold on their outstretched wings a box containing two satirical masks, and in the beak a necklace taken in the center by a palmette. The painting depicting two ducks on a yellow background, inserted between two green squares, is painted on the black frieze bordered by ornate ovule frames, alternating with lotuses.  79 N48532

A rear-facing heron is seen hovering on the lower left wreath, and a heron inspecting the bottom under its legs on the lower right. The lower edge of the suspended carpet is equipped with peacock feathers (a well-known lucky charm); the lower ends of the two thyrsis can be glimpsed placed on an ornament with gorgoneìon, in the center, reduced to only the outlines. Illuminated under the lower edge of the suspended carpet, two diverging hunts can be seen between animals running towards the side edges of the carpet: jumping antelopes behind, attacked by bulls.  79 N48355

Tablinum (i), S wall, section E, middle area: detail of the central painting, largely lost due to the hole made in the wall by the tunnels (which also caused the gap in the previous painting, in addition to the cracks in the whole wall). Only the upper left corner remains with two female figures under a Doric portico: probably an attendant and a noblewoman who in mourning tears her cut, white hair (sprinkled with ashes?). For Mau (BdiI 1876, p. 165) it is Hecuba mourning the body of Hector brought back to Troy. The epistyle of the aedicule, adorned with a palmette in the center and metopes with stylized motifs, is surmounted by a pediment with volutes filled with color and acroterial palmettes. The window above opens onto the interior of a thòlos with an Ionic colonnade, with a square coffered dome seen in perspective and a leafy opaìon adorned with four-petalled flowers. The element at the top of the white strip of the side panel is a zither: a pendant to the zither at the base of the strip, which also incorporates two rustic tortoise-shaped lyres with a head on the resonance box. Graphic rendering from Mau W, tav. XIII (detail).  79 E104521

51. Tablinum(s), S wall, section E, middle area, detail. The first heraldic 'pair' (from above) next to the palm trunk on the side of the central aedicule, is formed by two divergent groups of animals fighting: a deer that climbs the shoots in an attempt to escape the griffin that jumped on it that bites its back (left), neck (right). The red ellipse in the white strip is based on heart-forming scrolls that arise from the lyra rustica pentecorda, also with a tortoise-like resonance chamber with a head in the center.

52. Tablinum (i), S wall, section E, middle area, detail: the upper white frame with hanging lotuses of the central panel, with the leafy opaîon in the centre of the dome of the thòlos. The light shines from the left on the epistyle of the Ionic colonnade of the thòlos seen through the window, whose jamb E is highlighted by a white strip adorned with overlapping triangles.  79 N48528

53. Tablinum (i), S wall, O section, middle area, detail: painting depicting the busts of Maenad and Satyr on a blue background. The Maenad, who holds the Satyr embraced with her left hand, raises her right hand equipped with a bracelet, to place the crown on him. Already at the time of the excavation the painting was less well preserved than its counterpart (see fig. 49): according to Mau, these are paintings that "stand up to comparison with the most beautiful that have been found in this world" (Mau BdI 1876, p. 166). 79 N48346

54. Triclinium (u), wall N. The tablinum (1) is flanked by two triclinium overlooking the peristyle: (m) decorated in the fourth style together with the peristyle, and very ruined; (u) is frescoed like the tablinum in the III style, with a black plinth, a central aedicule with a red background with four columns, flanked by two yellow side panels both divided by a narrow black compartment with a candelabrum (see fig. below). The upper area has an architectural structure animated by avant-corps, with garlands and hanging tambourines. The centre of the wall, perforated as already seen on the S wall of the tablinum (see fig. 40), was closed after the excavation.

57. Peristyle (1), N portico, S wall with room door (s). The black plinth (above the access staircase to the cellar) is divided into three panels, adorned with plants and birds. The border of the carpet with two parallel lines of the two red panels of the middle area, separated by a narrow yellow compartment, indicates that the decoration is of the fourth style. Mau reports ample traces of gilding in the bracelets and earrings of the seated woman, in the net that covered her hair, and "on the yellow robe that covers her legs, and in the hair and on the upper arm of the standing figure" (Mau BdI 1876, pp. 228-229). 60. Peristyle (1), bottom section E. When the house was renovated in the first century A.D., the three conclavian (s), (r) and (t) were obtained from the E portico of the peristyle: of which the central one (r), entirely open to the viridarium, was accentuated by two columns erected in correspondence with the columns incorporated in the corners of the entrance to the exedra, and intended to support a tympanum with the intention of accentuating the environment,  located in the ideal axis of the house. These two columns, also erected in correspondence with those in the center of the O portico, are built in opus listatum with two rows of bricks and a row of tuff parallelepipeds, and covered with red plaster. The other columns are covered, in the lower third, with yellow plaster and white rudented stucco in the upper section. The Doric capital of the N-E column (on the left in the photo) is made of lava covered with stucco. The column of the $ corner of the entrance to the exedra (r) (right), made of fluted tuff with a chiselled Corinthian capital (see fig. 86), belongs to the construction phase of the house.

The hoof is red; the white middle area is divided into two panels with a border of carpet with staples, separated by yellow twisted candelabra. 89. Room (t), wall N. Central painting (Museo Naz. di Napoli, inv. 111213) depicting "A crowned Hermaphrodite, with an iridescent chlamys between yellow and green above both arms, so that the front part of the body remains uncovered, in the right hand a torch resting on the ground, stands upright, looking half to the right half towards the viewer,  and leaning with his left elbow on the shoulder of Silenus who was also crowned. The latter has a red robe around his legs with a blue lining and hem; a red flap hangs from the left arm, it is not distinguishable whether it is also on the shoulder; The shoes are yellow. He stands with his back to the Hermaphrodite, but turns his head to look at him; holds a drummer with his left hand, playing it with his right" (Mau BdI 1876, pp. 229-230).

91. Room (t), wall S. Central painting (Museo Naz. di Napoli, inv. 111214) depicting Aphrodite and Mars: "Mars with a helmet and red chlamys is seated on another red robe that wraps around his legs. He supports Venus' left elbow with his left, while his right holds a hem of a robe on the left. of her mother. The analogy of other paintings leaves no doubt as to the intention of this concept, namely, that he is about to take off her garment; but here that flap is not seen joined to the robe of Venus, and it could almost seem that Mars extends the right to support the goddess, at the same time holding a flap of her own garment. Behind the group described you can see a large quadrangular base" (Mau BdI 1876, p. 230).

93. V 1, 23. Triclinium (k), wall $, section W of the door. The recess in the wall is shaped according to the triclinium bed, with the pulvinus on the left (on the side of the door). These receipts were used to create more space in the central area intended for the canteen. The geometric pattern of the plinth continues uninterrupted in the recessing, as it was used in Roman wall schemes.

92. V 1,23. Atrium (b): view from the west, with the tuff impluvium belonging to the construction phase of the house (end of the third and beginning of the second century BC). The masonry base built behind the E edge of the impluvium is a function of the lead fistula that comes out of it at the top right. At the time of the excavation, everything was hidden under a black slate board with its two masonry supports. Between this and the impluvium there was "a monopodium of... travertine" which appears on the top right of the photo, on the edge of the wing(d) - "but without the board or basin that it was supposed to support, and broken at the top" (Mau BdI 1876, p. 232). The fistula "bending over the monopodium threw water into a travertine vase that is in the impluINS. 1, 23.26

94. V 1.23. Triclinium (k), wall N. The room was divided into an antechamber (in correspondence with the E section of the wall, on the right in the photo) and a room for triclinary beds (central and W section). This subdivision is reflected in the two different wall schemes, divided by a painted pillar. The poor state of conservation of the floor does not allow us to ascertain whether there was also a visual division here; in the N-W corner (on the left in the photo) there is a piece of cocciopesto adorned with crosses, typical of the end of the second century-first half of the first century BC. The plinth of the room is black with geometric ornamentation

95. V 1.23. Triclinium (k), N wall, central section of the triclinium room, detail: medallion with two concentric circles graffiti in the plaster, depicting a deer flying towards the W. It is located in the centre of a narrow compartment (now discoloured, perhaps it was on a black background), which separates two panels. The photo shows the calcite crystals mixed with the last surface layer, which makes up the pictorial film. Calcite replaced marble dust, which makes the frescoed surface as shiny as a silver mirror (speculum argenteum: Vitr., De Arch., 7.3.9).

96. V 1.23. Triclinium (k), wall E. Banqueters could enjoy the coolness of the shady courtyard (1) thanks to three overlapping windows that open into wall E: the large window covered with wooden mullions on the ground floor is dominated by a smaller splayed window with sguinci covered with white plaster, which captured the light at the top. This and the window above perform a structural function at the same time by unloading the weight of the wall on the architrave of the window below. The ceiling of the antechamber was therefore much higher than the vault of the hall, whose shutter was at the level of the side above the splayed window. The E wall of the courtyard (1) that can be seen from the window, is a rare example of opus caementicium made of irregular mouths of cruma rossa: lava foam stuffed with leucite, normally used in the III-I century BC for the upper floors and for the vaults, due to its slight specific weight. It is the back wall of the stable behind. 79 N48496

1. Façade: view from S-W. The photo illustrates well the juxtaposition of various types of housing in a Pompeian street, the Via Stabiana, with the entrance to the V 1, 29 workshop on the right next to the pillar with the N wall of bricks and tiles.

2. Façade, with the tile jambs of the door at no. 28 mortised 'in fins' in the lava opus incertum. The first floor has undergone a restoration in opus reticulatum with the jambs of the three windows in opus listatum. caption_en: 2. Atriotetrastilo (d), overall view from N. Four large Corinthian columns in tuff, fluted and covered with white and red plaster, partly fallen, with filled grooves and strips represented by two fillets, make up the valley, restored after the excavations. On the W side are visible the entrance to the room (h) and the entrance to the fauces (p), in the center the tablinum (0) and in the background the rhodium peristyle (r).

3. Atriot (d), overall view from S. On the W side the entrances to rooms (h) and (f) are visible, on the E side the entrance to the room (1). The square windows, above the aforementioned rooms, belong to a second floor obtained, thanks to a lowering of the rooms below, in a period subsequent to the first construction phase of the house.

4. Tetrastyle atrium (d): cocciopesto floor with regular dotted white tiles; on the N side two tank mouths are visible. The impluvium is made of tuff (type A1); on the S side there is a circular marble basin (diameter 78 cm) placed on a monopod, a rectangular base covered in marble and, behind this, a travertine puteal.
5. Tetrastyle atrium (d), compluvium: lion-headed sime in terracotta and palmette antefixes. The decorations were removed when the atrium roof was completed.
6a. Atrium tetrastyle (d): impluvium.

6b. Tetrastyle atrium (d), valley, S-E corner: details of the column and Corinthian capital ("Basilica" type), in gray tuff, which is repeated identically on the four columns and which has a basic collar with beads and spindles, two crowns of leaves, angular volutes wrapped in spirals under the smooth and quadrangular abacus with a bull. II/I century B.C.

7. The paintings in the atrium, probably after 62 AD, were subjected to restorations in the fourth style, especially in the plinth and in the middle area.

1. Atrium(s): the low impluvium with a molded kyma recta border (type A) reveals its antiquity in this detail and in the cocciopesto covering adorned with regular rows of white tesserae, dating back to the era of the first style. The $ plate allows you to see the mouth of the drain hole.

Atrium (e): of the rooms on the eastern side, almost devoid of pictorial covering, it is possible to grasp the masonry techniques: from the square work of the cubicle (k), to the uncertain work of the pantry (m) and the room (c') whose walls had to be repaired probably after the earthquake of 62 AD. The presence of lime heaps in (w) and (r), found at the time of the excavation, however, indicate that restoration work was underway in the building in 79 AD.

Cubicle (i), N wall: the scarce residues of the pictorial decoration with a black plinth and the middle area divided into panels, of which the red side ones, are now (1991) further reduced due to the fall of the plaster of the eastern section, which has brought to light a conspicuous brick closure of a pre-existing passage, the height of which reached the entire stretch of the preserved wall. On careful observation it is evident that the eastern wall, corresponding to the tablinum, was plastered and on it was placed the final section of the N wall, executed at a later time.
